Zereda
ZER-eh-dah
n. (the Ephraimite town of Jeroboam the son of Nebat)
Hebrew Tseredah, the cooling, or a piercing, from a root signifying to pierce or to be cool; named once, 1 Kings 11:26.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Zereda is named once, and its one claim on the record is the man who came from it: “And Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephrathite of Zereda, Solomon's servant, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow woman, even he lifted up his hand against the king” (1 Kings 11:26). Everything in the verse matters. He was an Ephraimite, of the tribe that would lead the northern secession; he was Solomon's own servant, promoted for his industry to be ruler over all the charge of the house of Joseph; his mother was a widow; and he lifted up his hand against the king. The LORD had already told him by Ahijah the Shilonite that ten tribes would be given him, and had attached a promise: if he would walk in God's ways and keep His statutes, God would build him a sure house as He built for David. Jeroboam received the kingdom and refused the condition. He made two calves of gold, set them in Bethel and Dan, said Behold thy gods, O Israel, and ordained a feast and a priesthood of his own devising. The phrase the sin of Jeroboam becomes the standing measure of apostasy for every northern king after him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Zereda, the Ephraimite town of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, named once, 1 Kings 11:26.

expand to see more

Hebrew Tseredah, the cooling, or a piercing.

It occurs once in the Authorized Version, 1 Kings 11:26.

The town of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, in the hill country of Ephraim.

His mother Zeruah was a widow woman of that place.

He was Solomon's servant before he lifted up his hand against the king.

Key Scripture

1Ki 11:26 — "And Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephrathite of Zereda, Solomon's servant, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow woman, even he lifted up his hand against the king."

1Ki 11:38 — "And it shall be, if thou wilt hearken unto all that I command thee, and wilt walk in my ways, and do that is right in my sight, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did; that I will be with thee, and build thee a sure house, as I built for David, and will give Israel unto thee."

1Ki 12:28 — "Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt."

1Ki 14:16 — "And he shall give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, who did sin, and who made Israel to sin."

Modern Corruption

Jeroboam's calves are excused as a cultural contextualising of Israel's worship; Scripture names them the sin that destroyed the northern kingdom.

expand to see more

Jeroboam did not announce a new god. He said, Behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt — claiming to represent the LORD who did the exodus, in a form the people would find accessible and in locations more convenient than Jerusalem. That is contextualisation, and Scripture calls it the sin whereby he made Israel to sin. The modern parallel needs no drawing out: worship redesigned for reach, with the God of the Bible still named over it.

The regulative principle is the safeguard, and the Second Commandment is its ground. God had appointed one place, one altar, one priesthood and one order of feasts, and Jeroboam altered every one of them for reasons of state. He had been given an explicit promise of a sure house on condition of obedience, and he traded it. A town called Zereda in the hills of Ephraim is remembered for producing the man by whom the measure of Israel's apostasy is named.
